title: Bangkok Struggles With Worst Flooding in 15 Years as Water Recedes
excerpt: Some 320 mm of rain in two to three days left waist-deep water across the capital, killed at least eight nationwide, stranded Thai Airways passengers, and could shave 0.3 points off GDP growth.
body:
• Bangkok was hit by about 320 mm of rain in two to three days late last week — nearly as much as the low-lying capital usually gets in all of September — submerging neighbourhoods in waist-deep water and overwhelming the drainage network.
  • All 50 districts were declared disaster zones. At least 8 people have died nationwide since September 16, more than 580,000 homes have been disrupted, and some 329,000 households in Bangkok are affected.
  • Suvarnabhumi Airport kept flights moving, but Thai Airways suffered severe baggage chaos — 34 flights delayed Monday, eight cancelled Tuesday — prompting the board to fire the airline's CEO.
  • The floods could cause economic damage of at least 11 billion baht ($327 million), and economists say they could shave 0.3 percentage points off Thailand's GDP growth this year.

BANGKOK — Thousands of residents sheltered in evacuation centres in Bangkok this week as parts of the Thai capital remained under floodwater days after 320 mm (12.6 inches) of rain fell in two to three days — nearly as much as the sprawling city usually gets in all of September, according to Reuters.

Entire neighbourhoods were inundated. Residents waded through waist-deep water in the hard-hit district of Bang Kapi to buy essentials from vendors, some of whom set up stalls with floating plastic boxes and drums.

"Over 80,000 residents living in flooded areas are unable to leave their homes," Unsit Sampuntharat, the permanent secretary of the interior ministry, said in a statement, adding that mobile kitchens and boats were being mobilised for relief. The goal, he said, is to provide three meals a day to all residents through the flooding period and for at least seven days after the waters recede.

Context & Background

The rain came from an area of low pressure that moved up the Gulf of Thailand and stalled over central Thailand for about two days. Canals across Bangkok burst their banks and flooded the roads alongside them, with the eastern part of the capital hit hardest.

On September 26, authorities declared a flood disaster emergency and designated all 50 of the capital's districts as disaster-affected areas. It is the worst flooding to hit Bangkok in 15 years. The geography is unforgiving: the capital sits on soft clay just 1.5 metres above sea level and is sinking by several millimetres a year, while more than 8.4 million people live through its six-month rainy season.

The crisis extends well beyond the capital. Floods have hit 41 provinces across Thailand since September 16, killing at least eight people and disrupting more than 580,000 homes, the interior ministry said. Further east, in the coastal province of Rayong abutting a major industrial belt, authorities ordered evacuations on Monday after two reservoirs swelled beyond capacity.

"The flooding is expected to shave 0.3 percentage points off this year's GDP growth, reducing growth to 2.1%, and cut third-quarter growth by about 0.5 percentage points to 1.7%."

— Aat Pisanwanich, economist at Rangsit University

Impact & Analysis

The floods could cause economic damage of at least 11 billion baht ($327 million) nationwide, economist Aat Pisanwanich told Reuters, with Bangkok and the eastern region taking the brunt — particularly wholesale and retail businesses. The timing hurts: Thailand's economy has lagged regional peers since the pandemic, expanding 1.9% year-on-year in the second quarter, down from 2.8% the previous quarter.

Although Suvarnabhumi Airport kept running, baggage handling was severely hit — 69 Thai Air Force personnel were called in on Monday to support Thai Airways ground operations after staff could not reach work through the water. The airline said 34 flights were delayed on Monday, baggage from 52 flights between September 26 and 27 was stranded, and eight flights were cancelled on Tuesday. The fallout reached the boardroom: the board fired CEO Chai Eamsiri after the operational meltdown.

Diaspora Angle

Bangkok is one of the most-visited cities on the planet for Indian travellers, and the floods landed squarely in that stream: Thai Airways cancelled routes including New Delhi, left passengers waiting six to eight hours for baggage, and warned of further schedule changes. Anyone with family in Bangkok should check flight status directly with the airline before heading to the airport. Beyond tourists, Bangkok's long-standing Indian business and trading community sits in the wholesale and retail districts expected to take the heaviest economic hit.

What's Next

The Thai government said on Tuesday that Bangkok's standing water should clear within two to three days if there is no additional rainfall, with none anticipated. The cabinet is set to discuss long-term flood plans and recovery measures. The deeper question is whether the worst-flooding-in-15-years episode forces investment in the drainage capacity of a city that keeps sinking — last year's catastrophic southern floods, which killed at least 145, showed how much higher the stakes can go.
